🎥 Day 13 Development Log

Context:

A museum may want to license the model for an interactive exhibit: museum-goers could pick a dinosaur species and watch its fossil record “rewind” through deep time. That means one thing: I needed a clean, high-resolution animation running from 0–70 Ma.
Today was about building that demo pipeline from scratch and untangling every obstacle between “I have the code” and “I have a polished video.”

And what a battle today was... because the final animation looks amazing.

🛠️ Technical Wins
• Created a dedicated museum-demo branch
	Finally separated demo-specific development from the main branch. Branching properly let me experiment freely without contaminating core logic.
• Tuned the reconstruction window for museum playback
	Reduced the time window to 0–70 Ma
	Increased temporal resolution from 10 Ma → 5 Ma for smoother movement
	This gave the animation the fidelity required for exhibition use.
• Built the entire export pipeline end-to-end
	The original run_animation() only saved individual PNG frames when export=True.
	No GIFs, no MP4s — nothing assembled.

	I had two options:
	- Rewrite the animation system to produce GIFs directly
 	- Export PNG frames, then stitch them into a video

	I chose the second because GIF = horrific compression → blurry coastlines.
	MP4 was the right choice for scientific visualization and museum playback.
• Added export_movie.py and integrated with animation
	This module handles:
	- sanitizing filenames
	- feeding frames into ffmpeg
	- producing a clean MP4 with correct resolution
• Installed and configured ffmpeg (after a hunt)
	At first ffmpeg “didn’t exist” on the system despite installation.
	Suspected PATH issues → correct.
	A full machine reboot fixed the environment variable resolution.
• Solved the “input images not found” error
	The cryptic 3752568763 error turned out to be a red herring.

	The real issue:
	ffmpeg refuses to process frames whose width or height is odd.
	My frames were 1861×1006 — width was odd.

	Solution: enforce even dimensions in the code.
• Fixed the one-frame MP4 problem
	The MP4 only showed frame 0000, nothing else.
	Two issues:

	- Frame naming was incompatible with ffmpeg.
	  ffmpeg expects sequential integers (0000, 0001, 0002…).
	  Mine were spaced by 5 Ma (0000, 0005, 0010…).

	- Double saving was happening.
	  ui.py saved frame_0000Ma.png
	  animation.py saved frame_0000.png
	  ffmpeg read the wrong batch first and never progressed.

	The root cause:
	Plotting code should never save images.
	I stripped the rogue saving logic out of ui.py.
	Once image export was centralized in animation.py, the animation finally stitched correctly.
• Final result:
	A complete, smooth, accurate MP4 of Earth unwinding from 0–70 Ma, with fossils moving coherently with their tectonic plates.
	It looks beautiful.

Meta-Lessons
• Having worked on this project for awhile now, often errors arise not from the code itself, but from path-ing/directory issues

	Today’s blockers were:
 	- PATH issues
	- ffmpeg installation quirks
	- ffmpeg dimension rules
	- filename conventions
	- duplicate PNG outputs

	Not logic bugs — environment + pipeline bugs.

• When a new module, extension, software is used, it will bring its own conventions that may not be a priori obvious. 
GPlates was one example. FFmpeg is another with its input convention and dimensional requirements. 
Aside from reading all the documentation beforehand, this can really only be fixed by trial-and-error: 
bumping into obstacles and learning as they arise.

• it is absolutely acceptable to iterate upwards. One error is relaced by another? That's progress. 
It's a step closer to the answer.

• Coding hygiene actually matters when the system grows
	The stray frame-saving snippet in ui.py seemed harmless early on.
	Today it caused:
	- double images
	- mismatched filenames
	- broken ffmpeg assembly
	- an MP4 frozen on frame 0

	One small hygiene mistake → downstream havoc.
	A clean architecture pays off.

Conceptual Lessons
• The “dinosaurs in the ocean” issue is deeper than rigid vs deforming plates

	I finally saw fossil motion at fine resolution along the western margin of North America.
	The longstanding puzzle:
	Why do some theropod fossils rewind into the ocean?
	
	Initially I blamed rigid plate models.

	But at higher granularity, a new insight emerged:

	Some fossils are being reconstructed to crustal fragments that were later subducted beneath the San Andreas system.

	We have zero access to:
	- their paleotopography
	- their paleobathymetry
	- their uplift/subsidence state before subduction.

	In other words:
	we don’t actually know whether the “oceanic” position was above or below sea level at that time.

	This reframes the whole interpretation issue and is absolutely worth discussing with Prof. Erin Saupe.

Up Next
1. Keep modern fossil locations fixed
	Museum viewers must see:
	- modern-day fossil positions
	- fossils rewinding backwards in time without “phasing out” based on species lifespan.

2. Switch PBDB filtering from clade-level → species-level
	Move from “Theropoda” to specific taxa: Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops horridus, etc.

3. (Optional) Dynamic legend generation
	Based on which species are included in reconstruction.

4. (Optional) Experiment with deforming plate models
	Direct comparison: Müller 2022 rigid model vs deforming models with partitioned crustal motion
	Useful for interpreting movement along margins like western North America.

But for the purposes of a museum demo... I've already produced the output I need :)
